title: About The Green Yard
text:
Planting a Sweet Granadilla




My name is Schuyler Hamilton and I am a native Arizonan. I absolutely love Phoenix and after living in mutiple states around the country during College I decided to come back to my home. Growing up my mom used to garden, we would grow all kinds of vegetables and they also had several mature citrus trees (Navel Orange, Grapefruit and Mandarin) in their Green Yard. This exposed me to the world of growing your own food. During High School and College I got away from gardening and focusing on other aspects of life including Photography and Videography. My oldest son was born in 2018 and my life was never the same again. Not only did he change every aspect of living but I also awakened my passion for growing my own food. In early spring of 2019 I bought my first Banana plants (Blue Java and Dwarf Nam Wah) and planted them in our old Green Yard.

Implemented new strategies that increased efficiency by 30%.
Led a team of 10 professionals in achieving project milestones.




Office Team







Studied Computer Science with a focus on artificial intelligence and machine learning.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is PACKED with Tropical Diversity!
text:
This Florida Food Forest Is PACKED with Tropical Diversity!

  
    Florida
    Tampa
    Food Forest Tours
    Tropical Fruit
    Zone 10A
    Gonza Gardens
  

  
    Tour the backyard of Gonza Gardens in Tampa, Florida, where KC grows an extraordinary collection of tropical fruit, perennial vegetables, pollinator plants, and rare ornamentals in USDA Zone 10A.
  

  

    
      Host
      KC at Gonza Gardens
    

    
      Published
      July 10, 2026
    

  




In Part 2 of our visit to Gonza Gardens, KC takes us through the backyard, side yard, raised beds, nursery propagation area, and an astonishing collection of tropical and subtropical plants growing in Tampa, Florida. This is a densely planted home food forest where fruit trees, perennial vegetables, rare ornamentals, wildlife habitat, and plant propagation all share the same space.




  
    Garden
    Gonza Gardens
  

  
    Host
    KC
  

  
    Location
    Tampa, Florida
  

  
    Climate
    USDA Zone 10A
  

  
    Garden Age
    Approximately 4 Years
  

  
    Tour Area
    Backyard and Side Yard
  





A Backyard Filled With Tropical Diversity


KC and her family originally began developing the backyard as a garden filled with rare ornamentals collected from around Florida. As their interest in food forestry grew, edible plants were layered into the existing landscape, creating a garden where beauty, food production, and wildlife habitat all overlap.



The result is not a conventional orchard with widely spaced trees. Mangoes, sapodillas, mulberries, avocados, white sapotes, jackfruit relatives, perennial vegetables, flowering plants, vines, ponds, and nursery stock are fitted into nearly every available part of the property.



Many of the trees are pruned to remain reachable, while grafting is used to grow several proven varieties on a single tree. Upper-canopy plants provide shade and protection for more sensitive species underneath them, helping KC grow plants that would otherwise struggle in Tampa’s occasional cold weather.






What You’ll Learn



  
    How KC layers fruit trees, shrubs, vines, ornamentals, and perennial vegetables into a small residential property
  

  
    Why grafted trees can provide more reliable fruit than unknown seedlings
  

  
    How pruning keeps mulberries and avocados productive and easy to harvest
  

  
    How water features support birds, frogs, lizards, pollinators, and other garden wildlife
  

  
    Why Florida gardeners often need tropical alternatives to lettuce, apples, peaches, pears, and other temperate crops
  

  
    How canopy cover and warmth from the house protect sensitive plants such as coffee and cacao
  







Five Highlights From the Tour



  
    
      
      
    
    
      This Tropical Fruit Replaces Apples in Tampa
      KC explains why jujube is a productive tropical alternative to apples in a climate with very few chill hours.
    
  

  
    
      
      
    
    
      Florida’s Most Underrated Fruit Tree?
      White sapote is cold tolerant, productive outside the main summer fruit season, and still unfamiliar to many growers.
    
  

  
    
      
      
    
    
      One of the Coolest Flowers in a Food Forest
      Dutchman’s pipe produces unusual flowers and serves as a host plant for the Polydamas swallowtail butterfly.
    
  

  
    
      
      
    
    
      Grow a Pineapple Patch From Store-Bought Tops
      Store-bought pineapple tops can be rooted and replanted, eventually becoming an expanding patch of homegrown pineapples.
    
  

  
    
      
      
    
    
      This One Tree Grows Three Different Mulberries
      KC shows how Shangri-La, Chiang Mai 60, and Skinner mulberries can all grow together on one grafted tree.
    
  







Growing With Florida’s Climate Instead of Fighting It


One of the strongest lessons from Gonza Gardens is the importance of choosing plants that actually want to grow in the local climate. KC explains that many of the apples, peaches, plums, pears, lettuces, peppers, and large tomatoes they initially tried were poorly suited to Tampa’s heat and limited winter chill.



Instead of repeatedly struggling with those crops, the garden now relies more heavily on subtropical and tropical alternatives. Jujube fills a role similar to a small apple, while moringa, katuk, longevity spinach, Okinawa spinach, and edible hibiscus provide perennial leafy greens that are better adapted to Florida’s heat.



White sapote is especially valuable because it tolerates cooler weather and can provide fruit outside the main mango-heavy summer season. This helps spread harvests across more of the year rather than having everything ripen during the same few months.






Pruning, Grafting, and High-Density Planting


KC keeps several trees intentionally small. Mulberries are repeatedly pruned because fruit growing beyond reach becomes bird food, while everbearing varieties such as Chiang Mai 60 can flower and produce again following pruning.



Grafting also allows the garden to hold more varieties without requiring a separate mature tree for every cultivar. One mulberry carries three varieties, while sugar apple, white sapote, and other trees are being top-worked or grafted to improve fruit quality, pollination, and overall reliability.



Because the property is densely planted, KC considers the future growth habit and vigor of each tree. Slow-growing star apples can be planted relatively close and trained in opposite directions, while fast-growing canopy trees such as ice cream bean and Cecropia are given roles in the upper layer.






Designing for Wildlife


The garden is designed to feed more than people. Firebush, porterweed, firespike, powderpuff, cassia, Dutchman’s pipe, dill, citrus, and other plants attract or support hummingbirds, butterflies, caterpillars, and pollinating insects.



KC also intentionally provides water through ponds and fountains. She has observed that birds may damage less fruit when clean drinking water is readily available. The same water features also support frogs, lizards, neighborhood cats, and the larger backyard ecosystem.



Rather than seeing insects and wildlife as separate from the garden, Gonza Gardens treats their interactions as part of a functioning food forest.

The Green Yard Takeaway




Gonza Gardens demonstrates that abundance is not simply a matter of owning more land. KC creates abundance through variety, intelligent pruning, grafting, climate-appropriate plants, multiple canopy layers, and a willingness to experiment.



The property produces food while also supporting hummingbirds, butterflies, frogs, lizards, and other wildlife. Even cold damage becomes part of the learning process, helping the garden evolve toward plants and protection strategies that are better suited to Tampa’s climate.








Food Forest Finds


KC and her family also operate Food Forest Finds, an edible plant nursery specializing in plants that have performed well in their own Tampa food forest. Many of the plants are propagated directly from material growing on the property.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
The Story
A food forest does not need to occupy several acres to contain remarkable diversity.
In this Florida garden, KC has used approximately 0.17 acres to grow an extensive collection of tropical fruit trees and edible plants. The tour offers a close look at how plants can be layered, grouped, and fitted into a residential landscape without treating each tree as an isolated specimen.
This section can later become the complete written story of the garden, including how KC began growing, how the property developed, the biggest challenges, and the ideas visitors can apply in their own yards.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
What Makes This Garden Abundant?
The defining feature of this food forest is its density.
Rather than leaving large open spaces between individual trees, the garden uses vertical layers and close planting to create room for a much wider range of edible species. That approach allows a small property to function as an unusually diverse living collection.

title: This Florida Food Forest Is Packed with Tropical Diversity
text:
Growing Lessons From This Tour

Small properties can hold considerable diversity.
Vertical layers help make better use of limited growing space.
Dense planting can create a food-forest environment rather than a conventional orchard layout.
Plant selection and placement matter when many species share a small area.
A residential landscape can become both productive and highly diverse.
